metadata.title: Match The Transport, Not The Key.
metadata.subtitle: The MCP Integration Skill (Transports & Tool Names)
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: when you wire an external service into a Claude Code plugin over MCP, is there one standard way to hook it up — or does the right setup depend on where the service actually runs? Lands the carry-out that the transport is matched to where the service lives, and the pre-allowed tool name has to match character for character or it fails silently.

beats.narration_text: You reach for 'key,' as if the credential is the choice that matters. It isn't — a plugin picks a transport, and that decides everything else. So: what transport does my plugin need for a service?

beats.narration_text: Four transport types, and every server picks exactly one. Here's what each one actually does. Stdio — Claude Code spawns a local process, talks to it over standard input and output, and shuts it down when it's done; that's for custom servers you wrote and local tools. SSE — a long-lived connection to a hosted server with OAuth handled for you: you log in once in a browser, and Claude Code manages the tokens after that; that's the shape for official hosted services like GitHub or Linear. HTTP — a REST call with a token in the request headers, for stateless one-off work, no session held open. WebSocket — a live, two-way socket for real-time updates. Here's the design choice worth naming: all four load lazily. Nothing connects until you actually use one of that server's tools, and a config change doesn't take effect until you restart. They optimized for cheap startup at the expense of fast feedback when a config is wrong.

production_viz.label: FOUR TRANSPORT TYPES
production_viz.caption: one per server, matched to where it lives

beats.narration_text: A few patterns keep a multi-server plugin from turning into a mess. Put server config in its own .mcp.json file instead of burying it inline in plugin.json — the config stays isolated, and adding servers doesn't churn the plugin manifest. Use CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT for every file path, never a hardcoded one — that variable resolves at load time, so the plugin still works after it's installed somewhere else. And when a command pre-allows tools, list the exact tool names instead of a wildcard — the format is mcp, double underscore, the plugin name, the server name, double underscore, the tool name, all stitched together. Here's what's actually happening: those names come from the running server, not from your config, so the only way to know them is to run slash-mcp first and read them off the live system.

Here's the catch, and it's the one worth naming: that tool name has to match character for character. Get one letter wrong in the pre-allow list, and the tool doesn't show up. No error, no warning — it's just not there. Same shape for credentials: for stdio or HTTP servers, they're plain environment variables, and nothing checks them until the first real call. A completely broken setup can look perfectly healthy right up until that moment. This works if you value cheap startup; it fails if you want config errors surfaced the moment you save the file.

production_viz.label: WRONG BY ONE CHARACTER
production_viz.caption: a mismatch fails silently, not loudly

beats.narration_text: Match the transport to where the service actually lives — stdio for local, SSE for hosted OAuth, HTTP for tokens, WebSocket for real-time. Then pre-allow the exact tool name, because one character off and it fails silently, not loudly.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude Code: Add a GitHub SSE MCP server and a local custom stdio server to my plugin. Then run the design-check — three things. Did it put server config in its own .mcp.json, kept separate from plugin.json? Does every path use CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT instead of something hardcoded? And before it pre-allowed any tools, did it tell you to run slash-mcp first, to read the exact names off the running server? Fail one of those and the plugin isn't portable; fail the last, and the tools will look configured but never fire.

beats.narration_text: Here is a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. It gives any frontier LLM the full transport map from the video — the four transports, the .mcp.json layout, the CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT rule, and the exact-tool-name format — and asks it to draft a working two-server config: an SSE server for GitHub, and a local stdio server for a script the plugin ships. Go deeper: how would you add a WebSocket transport for real-time updates without breaking the lazy-load contract the other three depend on, and what handshake would the local stdio server carry so it knows when to hand a long-running job off to that socket instead of blocking a stdio call?

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to add MCP servers to a Claude Code plugin. A Claude Code plugin extends the CLI, and each MCP server it declares picks exactly one of four transports: stdio (Claude Code spawns a local process and talks to it over standard input and output — for custom servers or local tools), SSE (a long-lived connection to a hosted server with OAuth handled for you — for official hosted services like GitHub or Linear), HTTP (a plain REST call with a token in a request header — for stateless one-off work), or WebSocket (a live, two-way socket for real-time updates). Server config goes in its own .mcp.json file, not inline in plugin.json. Every file path uses the CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT variable, never a hardcoded path. Commands that use tools pre-allow them by their exact name, in the shape mcp__<pluginname>__<servername>__<toolname>; there is no wildcard, and one wrong character makes the tool silently unavailable. Draft the .mcp.json for a plugin that wires up two servers: (1) the official GitHub MCP server over SSE, and (2) a local custom server over stdio that runs a Python script the plugin ships (script path built from CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT). Then draft a plugin.json command block that pre-allows exactly the GitHub read-issue tool and the local server's one Python tool — leave the tool names as placeholders in the correct mcp__<plugin>__<server>__<tool> shape, and add a comment saying to run /mcp against a live install to fill in the real names before shipping.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: how would you add a WebSocket transport for real-time updates without breaking the lazy-load contract the other three depend on, and what specific handshake would you write into the local stdio server's body so it knows when to hand a long-running job off to a WebSocket instead of blocking a stdio call?
